title: Parallel vectors, collinearity and ratios
what_it_asks: You are given position vectors or points, sometimes on a diagram. You are asked to find a vector between points, show that vectors are parallel or points are collinear, or find a point that divides a line in a given ratio. The idea is that parallel vectors are scalar multiples of each other, and that a point on a line can be written using a ratio or a scalar.
typical_structure: Usually two or three parts, worth about six marks in total. An early part asks you to find a vector such as $\overrightarrow{AB}$ in $\mathbf{i}$, $\mathbf{j}$, $\mathbf{k}$ form or in terms of given vectors. A later part then uses it to show a parallel or collinear result, or to find a position vector from a ratio. Some questions have a diagram. Later parts often rely on the vector found earlier.
mark_pattern: Most parts are short. A 2-mark part is usually M1 A1: a method mark for a correct subtraction or ratio set-up, then an accuracy mark for the correct vector or value. A 3-mark part is often M1 dM1 A1: form the vectors, then make the scalar-multiple or coefficient comparison, which depends on the first method, then the accuracy mark. Some parts are M1 M1 A1. Show-that parts typically end M1 A1*, where the last mark needs a complete argument and a conclusion. A few 1-mark parts are B1 for a stated vector. A 4-mark part can run M1 A1 dM1 A1.

where_marks_leak.text: You find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ as $\overrightarrow{OA} - \overrightarrow{OB}$, so the vector has the wrong sign. The M1 for the subtraction is lost, and the A1 and any dM1 that depend on it go too.
You round a length or value to the wrong number of significant figures or decimal places, or round too early. The final A1 is lost even though the method was sound.
You make a numerical slip in a component while subtracting or scaling. The A1 is lost, although follow-through may still help later marks.
In a shape or angle part, you use the wrong rule or pair a side with an angle that is not opposite it. The M1 is lost, and the accuracy mark after it goes too.

write_to_earn: Write $\overrightarrow{AB} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}$ (end minus start) before you put in numbers, so the method mark is safe.
For a parallel or collinear result, write one vector as a scalar multiple of the other and state the scalar.
For a ratio, write the position vector as a starting point plus a fraction of the line vector, then simplify.
In a show-that part, write the step just before the printed result and finish with a conclusion in words, such as the points lie on one line.
Keep components exact and round only in the final line, to the accuracy asked for.
check_before_you_leave: Ratio parts in the right order
